The Anchorage Assembly was scheduled this week to debate and potentially vote on a zoning proposal intended to add density within many of Anchorage’s established neighborhoods. Strongly divided public opinion and a new, last-minute version of the ordinance further delayed a final decision Wednesday. With a substitute version now on the table and a “raft” of proposed changes, sponsor Erin Baldwin Day said she wanted members on the same page before entering a discussion. Members unanimously agreed to pause further discussion until Nov. 4. “Especially with something as weighty as Title 21 (the city’s land use code) ... we owe it to the public and ourselves to do that work thoroughly before getting into debate,” Baldwin Day said Thursday. The proposal, called the Missing Middle Housing Opportunity overlay, or MMHOP, targets housing developments that fall in between traditional single-family homes and dense apartment buildings: townhomes, duplexes, triplexes and cottage-court style homes that typically serve young working professionals, students and older adults seeking to downsize. MMHOP would allow more, and in some cases, taller units on a single lot and reduced how far a new build must be set back from adjoining properties and the street.

In response to public feedback, co-sponsors Baldwin Day and George Martinez included “neighborhood-compatible” height limits and lot sizes and a 30-foot height restriction in single-family neighborhoods. On Tuesday, member Janice Park, who represents Midtown alongside Baldwin Day, introduced a new version of MMHOP. Park and Baldwin Day’s district encompasses neighborhoods such as Rogers Park, where residents have been vehemently opposed to the proposed zoning changes. “We’ve heard from a lot of people of a lot of concerns,” Park said. “They deserve to have been heard, and I’m willing to work with anybody to produce a policy that is the most advantageous to the community.

Park’s version contains a five-tiered approach to adding density where traditional single-family neighborhoods would accommodate “gentle infill” such as accessory dwelling units, duplexes and cottage courts. It permits multi-plexes and low- and mid-rise apartments in mixed residential and more urban areas. Park’s proposal also creates a 10-year sunset if the zoning overlay does not contribute to at least 30% of the municipality’s 10-year housing targets, and if added density impairs winter snowplowing or emergency vehicle access — two complaints frequently made by those opposed to MMHOP.

Three members of the Anchorage Assembly have introduced a measure that would add criminal penalties when people sleep or camp in public areas in the city, including parks, trails and sidewalks. The ordinance, AO 2025-74, will hear public testimony at the Assembly’s regular meeting next week, even after recent signals from officials that it would be costly to enforce and likely to invite legal challenges if implemented. The sponsors are South Anchorage’s Keith McCormick, as well as Jared Goecker and Scott Myers, both of whom represent Eagle River.

The measure adjusts Anchorage’s criminal code to bar “sleeping or establishing temporary living quarters, including, but not limited to, erection of a tent or other shelter” on public parcels, which includes “streets, highways, sidewalks, alleys, transportation facilities, parking areas, convention centers, sports arenas, schools, plazas, parks, and playgrounds.” Under the city’s abatement protocols, notices are first posted around an encampment telling people they need to leave, usually within 10 days, though sometimes fewer if there’s a risk to public safety.
